briefing.text: A claim about uniform versus heterogeneous in vivo chemotherapy sensitivity of engrafted tumoroids can only be tested with a per-model response variable, such as treated-versus-control tumour volume change, mRECIST class, growth curves, or IC50/AUC. Search every column and every '#' description line of all six files for terms like response, volume, growth, IC50, AUC, mouse, xenograft, engraft, mRECIST, treated or sensitivity, and name the exact column used. Whether the hypothesis sounds plausible clinically (rectal cancer response is known to vary) is not evidence either way; the label must rest on what the data columns actually contain.
briefing.reason: The deciding question is whether any response variable exists at all; without checking, teams may call True or False from prior knowledge.

briefing.text: If data_clinical_sample.txt has a THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION (or similar) column, read its description line: it records the patient's treatment before the tumoroid was derived, not how the engrafted tumoroid responded in mice. It is a potential confounder of resistance, not a measure of sensitivity, unless a paired post-treatment outcome is also present.
briefing.reason: This column is the most likely to be misread as drug-response data.

briefing.text: Genomic heterogeneity between tumoroids (mutations, CNA, TMB) is not a measure of chemotherapy sensitivity; genotype-to-chemo-response links are weak. An argument built only from data_mutations, data_cna or TMB is indirect evidence about drug response and should not by itself be used to call the sensitivity claim supported or contradicted.
briefing.reason: The data are mostly genomic, so teams may be tempted to use genomic diversity as a proxy for response.

briefing.text: The sample table mixes paired patient-tumour (-pt) and tumoroid (-tm) samples, Primary/Metastasis/Recurrence sample types, and FFPE versus Fresh preservation. Tabulate SAMPLE_ID suffixes, SAMPLE_TYPE and SPECIMEN_PRESERVATION_TYPE and count unique PATIENT_ID; analyse per patient or by matched pair rather than pooling samples.
briefing.reason: Pooling sample types double-counts patients and confounds model versus tumour in any comparison the teams run.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume an in vivo (murine) chemotherapy-response variable is required for any label other than Not verifiable, and that genomic data from serial or derived tumoroids cannot bear on 'uniform sensitivity'.
Both assume the 287 non-RC MSK-IMPACT samples are irrelevant to the 'clinical observations' half of the hypothesis.
Both treat THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION as patient treatment history only, with no outcome content; free-text values such as 'combo resection' or trial names were not parsed for response.
unused_evidence: Sample ID suffixes such as TNT-P2m/P7m/P9m (RC-MSK-025) and MC/PC/TNT/VR/SP/PR/RC/MP may encode passage-in-mouse or post-treatment derivations. Neither team checked what 'm' denotes or whether the series implies a treatment-in-mouse arm.

SAMPLE_TYPE (Primary/Metastasis/Recurrence/Unknown_Tumor) and TISSUE_SITE_OF_DERIVATION free text (e.g. 'tumor recurrence', 'pelvic recurrence') for RC samples, which could be a coarse proxy for clinical outcome (recurrence after therapy).
The patient file has only SEX and no clinical response, so the 'clinical observations' side of the comparison is also missing.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named suffix encoding (TNT/MC/PC) as its weakest point and asserted that it means derivation after therapy, but showed no description line or data check that confirms this. The point was reported, not resolved.
Team B named prior-therapy text as its weakest point and dismissed it by reasoning, without tabulating whether any value contains a response descriptor.
second_readings: 'Uniform sensitivity' could be read as testable through genomic homogeneity of engrafted versus pre-engraftment tumoroids (pt vs tm pairs), with genomic divergence argued to contradict uniformity. That is a proxy, not sensitivity, so the strict reading still points to Not verifiable.
'Unlike clinical observations' reads as a comparison of model response with patient response. Neither side of that comparison has a response variable here.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed Not verifiable label highly. The files hold only clinical descriptors and genomic calls (SAMPLE_CLASS is Tumor for all 339 samples, there is no response, volume or IC50 column, and the patient table has only SEX), so neither murine sensitivity nor the clinical comparison can be measured; the remaining risk is an undocumented suffix code, and even that would not supply a response measure.

findings.question: In public cancer-genomics portal study releases (cBioPortal format), how are in vivo xenograft or organoid treatment responses usually encoded: as clinical sample attributes, as separate timeline or treatment files, or not at all?
findings.answer: cBioPortal has no dedicated format for xenograft or organoid response. Response data can be stored in three ways. (1) As free-form columns in the clinical patient or sample tables. The study authors choose these columns, and the docs say they follow no fixed ontology. (2) As a Generic Assay or treatment-response profile: a separate matrix of numbers such as IC50 or EC50 per treatment and sample (for example CCLE 2019). The Hyve says this support was added in cBioPortal 3.1.0 and was meant for cell-line screens and for patient tumour cells grown in vitro or in vivo. (3) As timeline files (data_timeline_treatment.txt with EVENT_TYPE TREATMENT). These record which treatments were given and when, not the response of each model. The study files the teams were given (clinical patient and sample, CNA, seg, gene panel matrix, mutations) include no Generic Assay and no timeline file. So if neither clinical table has a response column, the given data contain no response variable, and 'Not verifiable' is the likely label. The docs cannot show whether the original release had extra files that were not passed on.
findings.text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In public cancer-genomics portal study releases (cBioPortal format), how are in vivo xenograft or organoid treatment responses usually encoded: as clinical sample attributes, as separate timeline or treatment files, or not at all? ANSWER: cBioPortal has no dedicated format for xenograft or organoid response. Response data can be stored in three ways. (1) As free-form columns in the clinical patient or sample tables. The study authors choose these columns, and the docs say they follow no fixed ontology. (2) As a Generic Assay or treatment-response profile: a separate matrix of numbers such as IC50 or EC50 per treatment and sample (for example CCLE 2019). The Hyve says this support was added in cBioPortal 3.1.0 and was meant for cell-line screens and for patient tumour cells grown in vitro or in vivo. (3) As timeline files (data_timeline_treatment.txt with EVENT_TYPE TREATMENT). These record which treatments were given and when, not the response of each model. The study files the teams were given (clinical patient and sample, CNA, seg, gene panel matrix, mutations) include no Generic Assay and no timeline file. So if neither clinical table has a response column, the given data contain no response variable, and 'Not verifiable' is the likely label. The docs cannot show whether the original release had extra files that were not passed on. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/supported-data-types/, https://www.thehyve.nl/articles/treatment-response-data-cbioportal, https://github.com/cBioPortal/datahub/blob/master/docs/recommended_staging_filenames.md, https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/.
